p: Ken found two tables in Lumen's staging seed that had never been scrubbed, and Copilot had been reading them.
The folder had come over in Priya's July migration, marked already scrubbed. She said it was hers before anybody asked.
Ken fenced the folder off from Copilot, and the team learned where that fence doesn't reach, like agent mode in the editor.
Priya talked Joyce out of telling the board that Copilot couldn't see patient data anywhere. The true version had a folder in it.
By Friday the real rows were gone, replaced with invented ones, and Ken and Priya both signed that the fence held.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. He just installed Copilot in his terminal, and he's the one asking now.
Ken Ito. Security lead. The switches are his.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. He asks before he does things now, mostly.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer. She owns the team's fixtures prompt now.
Tomasz Nowak. Leads Kraków. His people start work while Denver sleeps.
Nora Kim. Compliance. She wants every number traceable to its source.
Anders texted on Sunday night at 11:40, which for Anders was early. installed the copilot thing in my terminal. it says halcyon won't let me use it. fix that and I'll show you something.
Priya read it Monday at six with the kettle going and decided it was the nicest thing he'd said about Copilot since October.

At 6:30 Asha's five photos came in. Across the top card, in purple: Week seven. Standing orders. The doctor can't be at every bed, so she writes down what you're allowed to do without calling her. Learn them on your first night, not your worst one.

An email from Joyce Cho. Subject: Seats. Finance wants to know why we're paying for Copilot seats nobody's using. The invoice and last week's usage report are about thirty people apart. The billing cycle closes with the month. Can I have a real list by Friday? Real meaning right, not short. Joyce
She drove in thinking about the word real, and about Anders, who had never once texted her to come see something.
Asha's first card said: A standing order lets a nurse act without paging the doctor. Read every one before your first shift. The night you need it is a bad night to find out what it says.
The second card: On nights you had your rooms. You didn't walk into somebody else's patient just because the door was open.
The third card was underlined twice. A standing order names the drug, the dose, the route, and when. I never saw one that said use your judgment. That's what the phone call was for.
The fourth card: Report isn't the whole shift. It's what the next nurse needs, and nothing she doesn't.
The last card: Every shift started with a census. Who's here, who's leaving, and who's on the board but not in a bed.

At nine Anders put his laptop on her desk, open to a terminal. He'd installed the CLI on Sunday night with one npm command, typed copilot, signed in, and been told politely that his organization didn't allow it.
Ken was already standing behind him. He'd seen the laptop cross the room.

I left the CLI policy off in October. On purpose. Nobody had asked for it, and I don't turn on what nobody's asked for. He looked at Anders. Somebody's asking. Before it goes on, I want to know what it can reach.

Ken opens GitHub's table of which policies reach which surfaces before he touches the switch. Content exclusion applies to the CLI, the docs say, and he says he'll test that the way they did last week. The public code filter doesn't reach it. Its prompts are kept for 28 days. Then he sets Copilot CLI to Enabled, and the change lands in the audit log under his name. Anders types copilot again. Now it wants to know if I trust my home directory. Do you? Not even slightly.

Org seats follow the organization's Copilot policies, and the CLI has its own. An organization owner enables it in the Copilot policies settings, unless the enterprise already decided. Read what a surface reaches before you open it.
By ten the CLI policy was on.

Anders had typed copilot from his home folder, which was where his terminal always opened. Everything he'd touched in seven years was under there somewhere: a folder called src with a dozen repos in it, his SSH keys, a folder called taxes.
The CLI wanted to know if he trusted all that. His cursor was already sitting on choice two, the one that says remember this folder.
The Terraform's in Lumen. The deploy scripts live in their own repo. I want it to see both, and I'm not starting it twice.

He presses Esc, changes into the Lumen repository, and starts it there. When the work needs the deploy scripts, he types /add-dir with that path. That's two folders. The keys, the taxes, and ten other repos never come into it. Home is where I keep everything, he says. That's the problem with it.

Whatever folder you trust, Copilot may read, change, and run files in it and everything under it. So the CLI belongs in the project folder, not home, which GitHub warns against by name. /add-dir brings in a second folder mid session.
At two Anders asked her to come watch.
In October it explained my Terraform in the editor and got one thing backwards, he said. Let's see what it does in a terminal.

He typed: explain the staging database module. Copilot answered about the wrong one. There were three staging database modules under infra/modules: staging-db, staging-db-old, and staging-db-v2, which nobody had finished. The one he meant was plain staging-db, no ending on the name. He'd written it in 2019.
It had picked up the instructions file and his Terraform file on its own, rules and all. Wrong module anyway.

Point it at the file. An at sign, then the path. He types explain, then an at sign and the path to staging-db's main file, and Tab finishes the path for him. The answer walks the module from top to bottom: the instance, the backup window, prevent_destroy on the database. Then it quotes a comment he left in 2019 and forgot about. Don't shrink this below 100 GB, the restore needs room. He reads it twice. I wrote that for whoever came next. Something came next. He doesn't argue.

In Copilot CLI, plus a relative path, like @infra/modules/staging-db/main.tf, pulls that file into your prompt, and the path autocompletes. IDE chat flips it: is a participant there and is a file. Easy to mix up.
By Tuesday morning Anders's desk had become a place people stood. Devin was there with coffee. Renata had brought a chair.
Anders had asked the CLI to clear out old plan files from the drift checks. It wanted to start with one.

The Copilot CLI in lumen, Tuesday at 9:12. Anders asked it to delete the plan files in infra plans older than 30 days, and it wants to run rm, the delete command, on the first one, a staging plan from September second. It offers three choices: one, yes; two, yes, and approve rm for the rest of the running session; three, no, and tell Copilot what to do differently.
There were forty one files. I'm asking, not telling. Two, right? Devin said. Otherwise you're pressing one all morning.

Anders presses Esc and asks for a script that lists plan files older than 30 days and deletes them only when given a --delete flag. It writes cleanup-plans.sh. He runs it without the flag and gets forty one names. The last is the plan for Thursday's change, copied from a backup on Friday with September's date. He fixes the check, runs it again, then runs it with --delete. Two would've taken Thursday's too. Two would've taken anything called rm.

Approving a command for the rest of the session approves the tool, not just that command. Say yes to rm that way once and Copilot can run any rm until the session ends. For bulk file work, have it write a script you can read and dry run first.
Tuesday at three Tomasz called with his camera on. It was eleven at night in Kraków, and he'd waited up for this.

My team starts at seven. Twice this month they found drift in staging at ten, after building on it. I want a drift check waiting for them every morning. Your Anders says the CLI can do anything now. Can it do this every morning?
Behind him, on Kraków's own whiteboard, someone had copied Denver's two columns, agent mode on the left and the coding agent on the right, coffee cup and all.

Anders asks for a script that runs terraform plan with -detailed-exitcode in each workspace, prints one line per workspace, treats exit code 2 as drift, and never applies anything. It writes drift-check.sh in a minute. He reads every line, runs it against staging, and finds it skips a workspace with a space in its name. Copilot fixes the quoting. He opens a pull request, and Tomasz reviews it before he goes to bed. Good. A script does the same thing every morning. A prompt might get creative.

Copilot CLI is good at writing scripts. For a job that must run the same way every day, have it write one, then read, test, and review it like any other code. The script runs without a model, so it's the same every time.
Wednesday at ten Renata came to Priya's desk, because Anders was in a meeting and she'd decided not to wait.
She'd spent an hour in a CLI session in the Lumen repository, working through the infra folder module by module with Anders's checklist. Then her laptop had restarted for an update.
Is that hour just gone? I don't want to start over and explain it all again.

She types copilot --continue in the Lumen folder, and the hour comes back: her questions, the answers, the plan she'd started. It saved it? Sessions are saved. Continue takes the most recent one. Resume gives you a list. Renata names the session with /rename before she does anything else. Later she types /clear before an unrelated question, and Priya doesn't have to tell her why.
The CLI saves sessions. copilot --continue resumes the most recent one in that folder, and --resume or /resume lets you pick from a list, context included. Use /clear or /new between unrelated tasks.
Wednesday afternoon Anders was deep in staging-db, his 2019 module, splitting it into pieces he could test. He had four terminals open and the look he got when he didn't want to be talked to.
Tomasz messaged anyway. Thirty modules, thirty READMEs, all wrong since the summer. My new people read them first. Can Copilot fix them without stopping you?
Under it Tomasz added: Our whiteboard has editor and GitHub. Where does the terminal go?

Anders types /delegate update the README in each module to match its variables and outputs. The CLI offers to commit his unstaged work to a new branch as a checkpoint, then hands the task to the coding agent on GitHub, the one the docs now call the cloud agent. A link appears to a draft pull request and the agent's session. He goes back to the refactor. By five the pull request is waiting, thirty READMEs, two of them describing variables that don't exist. He mentions @copilot in a comment, and it fixes them. Terminal hands it to GitHub. I'll draw an arrow.

/delegate, or a prompt that starts with sends a task from the CLI to the cloud agent. It works in the background on a new branch and opens a draft pull request for your review. The CLI's autopilot mode works locally without asking, and agent mode works in the editor while you watch.
Thursday morning Devin brought her a single line on a sticky note, which was new for Devin.

I'm asking before I do it. The drift script finds drift. I want the CLI to fix it too, every night at ten, before Kraków starts. copilot -p, fix any drift in staging, with --yolo, because nobody's going to sit up to press yes. That's the whole point of it.
Across the room Anders stopped typing.
In October he'd written the rule himself and posted it under his own name: nobody approves a command they haven't read.
A flag that skips the yes or no question. Staging. Nobody watching.

The ten o'clock job stays the script, which changes nothing. When Kraków logs on, the report tells them which workspaces to leave alone, and each morning at 7:30 Devin opens a CLI session with the report attached, asks for a fix, reads the plan, and approves the apply himself. Anders comes over before Devin's back at his desk. In October I pressed Continue while I was on a call. That flag is the same button with nobody on the call. He adds one line to the draft of the team's CLI guide and puts his name after it: no allow all in any scheduled job.

Responsible use keeps a person on anything that changes state. A programmatic run can't stop to ask, so it shouldn't hold permission to make changes. Let automation report, and let people validate and apply.
Thursday at two Anders had a script for Joyce's list. He'd had the CLI write it in twenty minutes and had read it in twenty more.

What Anders's seat cleanup script does, in three steps. First a GET to the REST API's Copilot billing seats endpoint for the organization, which lists every seat, and then it keeps anyone whose last activity date is empty or more than 30 days old. Last, a DELETE to the billing selected users endpoint with those names, which puts those users' seats into pending cancellation.
Step two had found twenty eight people. Nora was reading the list over Priya's shoulder.

Hold on. Read it with me first. They read the list together, one name at a time. Six of the twenty eight turned telemetry off in their editors, and the activity date only shows editor use when telemetry is on. Priya has watched some of them use Copilot this week. Two more people are on leave until January. Take those eight off the list, and that leaves twenty. Anders runs the removal Friday morning. Listed by the API, checked by people, removed Friday, Nora says. An auditor can follow that.

The seats endpoint shows each seat's last activity, but IDE activity only appears when telemetry is on. A seat list is where you start. Check it with people before you remove access, then remove through the API.
Friday morning the removal ran for twenty people.
At eleven Nora brought her laptop over, open to the seat list from the API.
They're all still on here. Every one. The three I asked say Copilot still works. Did it fail? Finance reads this on the first.
Anders leaned in. Most of the removed names had a date beside them now. Four didn't.

They read the API's response together. A removed seat goes to pending cancellation, with a date, and access ends when the billing cycle does. The four without a date get Copilot through the infra team's assignment, so removing them as users changed nothing. Two of them left infra in the summer and were never taken off the team. The other two moved to integrations in October. Ken takes all four off the team. Nora writes it down. So the list is right. It's just early.

Removing users through the REST API sets their seats to pending cancellation, and they keep access until the billing cycle ends. Someone who also gets a seat through a team keeps it until they leave the team or the team's seat is removed.
Friday at two Renata found out she was joining the infra rotation in December. She went straight to Anders.
I have two weeks to learn the infra folder. How did you learn it?
I wrote it. He looked at Priya's old runbook on the corner of her desk, the one with his name in the margins. More of the ask Anders lines had a stroke of her pen through them every week.
Then he turned to Priya. You're running this. How should she learn it?

The way I should have learned it. Ask the CLI, then make terraform plan prove it. Bring Anders whatever's left. Renata starts in plan mode, which asks before it writes anything. She asks what each module does, which are still used, and what breaks if staging-db goes away. Then she runs terraform plan herself to see whether the answers hold. One doesn't: the CLI calls staging-db-old unused, and plan shows a backup job still pointing at it. By four she has seven questions for Anders, and none of them is where's the file. Those are the right questions. Those are the ones I can't put in a file.

Copilot speeds up learning a codebase and cuts context switching, because you ask about the code where you're working. Check what it says against the system itself, then bring a person the questions that need judgment.

At four she sent Joyce the list: twenty seats coming off, two people on leave keeping theirs, and six who'd turned telemetry off keeping theirs too. Joyce wrote back one line. That's what real looks like. Thank you.
At 5:10 on Friday Anders requested her review on a pull request: docs/cli.md, the team's guide to Copilot CLI, with a link to the Terraform instructions file at the top.
The first line said nobody approves a tool they haven't read. Under it, smaller: deny beats allow, so write the no first.
He came over before she'd opened it, and sat on the corner of the desk the way he used to when she was a data engineer and he was explaining something for the second time.
When I left in the spring, I gave you the platform and a runbook with all the hard parts missing. How many times did you write ask Anders in it?
That's twenty three things I should've written down and didn't. That was a bad handoff.
Not yet. Contracts end. Mine will. He tipped his chin at her monitor. Read it before you approve it. You've been the reviewer since October.

She read every line. She left one comment, on a sentence that said Copilot would ask before anything dangerous, and changed would to should. He accepted it from the corner of her desk without arguing, and she approved it.

Sunday was dinner in Aurora. Rice, measured to the first knuckle like always. Asha brought the cake from the bakery on Havana, the one she'd been calling worse every year since she moved down from Greeley.
Priya told them about the week. Forty one files, and a script that listed them before it deleted anything. Devin's ten o'clock job, and the flag that would have let it do anything it liked.

Her father put his fork down for the ten o'clock part. Second shift, the setup man wrote feed and speed on the sheet and went home. Your job was his numbers. Midnight, nobody around, foreman asleep in his truck. His numbers.
And if his numbers looked wrong?
Kill the spindle. Call him at home. He picked the fork back up. Earl. Hated the phone. Picked up every time, though, and never told one of us not to call.
Every standing order I ever followed had a phone number at the bottom, Asha said, and passed Priya the dal.

She caught every light on Colfax going home. In her own driveway, engine off, she opened the guide on her phone, scrolled past the last line Anders had written, and added one more. Then she typed her own name after it. If it looks wrong, stop it and call.
